payload.author: Vyacheslav-Tomashevskiy
payload.title: fix(hardware-db): make SPARC substring fallback conservative

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Reviewed against the real diff and a live 3-way merge into current `main` (not the PR's line counts).

**What actually lands.** The +1763/-81 in the description is a stale-base artifact: this branch was cut from `8952f23`, and `main` has since taken ~everything in the branch (the attestation-enforcement gate, MOS/Zilog weights, the warthog cap + settlement-rollback fix in anti_double_mining.py) via other PRs. A real `git merge` of the head into current `main` auto-merges with **no net change to the node file or anti_double_mining.py** — the only files that change are:
- `node/rustchain_hardware_database.py` (the fix, +19/-4)
- `node/tests/test_sparc_substring_fallback_conservative_poc.py` (new)

Heads-up on the GitHub merge-preview: because the merge ref is stale, it *appears* to delete `utxo_db.py`/`utxo_endpoints.py`/`test_utxo_dual_write_double_spend.py`. That is not real — the head branch never touches those files (empty diff vs. its own merge-base); those UTXO commits (incl. #8286) simply landed on `main` after this branch's base. A normal squash/merge preserves them.

**The fix is correct and fail-closed.** `lookup_hardware()`'s substring fallback now anchors an unidentified generation to the matched family's *minimum* base_multiplier instead of the first substring-matched row. Verified: `SPARC-T` → UltraSPARC III **2.5x** (was 3.0x LEGENDARY); exact keys like `ultrasparc_ii` still resolve to 3.0x; junk → `None`; `sparc_t` only substring-matches the `sparc` family, so no cross-family bleed. Correct direction, and low exposure — no SPARC has ever attested (#8237).

**Gates:**
- `scripts/check_fetchall.sh` on the merged tree: `OK: no new unannotated .fetchall()` (legacy baseline 171).
- `pytest node/tests/test_sparc_substring_fallback_conservative_poc.py`: 4 passed.
- `gh pr checks`: label / size-label / welcome all pass.

Verdict: **safe to merge** — genuine defensive fix, net change is the two files above. Leaving the actual merge to a human hand since this is node/attestation code.

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
The **core fix is excellent** — anchoring an unidentified SPARC generation to the family's cheapest multiplier (min by base_multiplier) is the right fail-closed direction, and the test is solid. Exact matches still short-circuit, so identified hardware is unaffected.

**Blocker before merge — please rebase.** The +1880 lines are two `chore: sync with upstream/main` commits, and that sync is stale. Merging as-is would revert two recent prod changes in the node file:
1. Deletes `_migrate_headers_columns()` + its init_db call (stops a fresh node crashing on the first signed header).
2. Reintroduces client-controlled `cpu_serial`/`hardware_id` into the `_compute_hardware_id` binding key — undoing the hardware-binding hardening (and the in-flight #71 fix in #8292), which is at odds with this PR's own reward-integrity goal.

`mergeable: MERGEABLE` only means no textual conflict. Please rebase onto latest main and drop both sync commits so the PR is just `rustchain_hardware_database.py` + its test. No rush — no SPARC has ever attested, so zero live exposure.

payload.author: L1nkinPark
payload.title: [UTXO-BUG] Skip mempool-claimed inputs in transfer coin selection

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Reviewed the real diff and the call path; ran the tests both ways.

**Confirmed real.** On `main`, `get_coin_select_candidates()` (utxo_db ~L456) returns every unspent box regardless of `utxo_mempool_inputs`, and `apply_transaction()` (~L849-859) then correctly refuses an input claimed by a different `tx_id`. So a pending claim on a dust box turns a fundable `/utxo/transfer` into a 500. Your test fails on `main` with `500 != 200 ... UTXO transaction failed (race condition or validation)` and passes on the PR head (`test_utxo_endpoints.py` + `test_utxo_db.py` -> 142 passed, 39 subtests). `get_coin_select_candidates` has exactly one caller (`utxo_transfer`), so the `NOT EXISTS` filter cannot change any other code path, and it is applied to both the cheapest and dearest slices so the bounded-selection argument in the docstring still holds.

Two notes, neither blocking:
1. `self.mempool_clear_expired()` now runs a `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` on every transfer call. That is one extra write-lock acquisition per transfer. Acceptable, but if transfer volume ever matters it could move to a periodic sweep.
2. When a wallet's *only* funds are mempool-claimed, the endpoint now returns 400 "Insufficient UTXO balance" while `balance_rtc` (from `get_balance`) still shows the claimed funds. Not wrong, slightly confusing; a `reserved_nrtc` field or a distinct code would make it self-explanatory.

**Context, not a criticism:** on the production node the UTXO blueprint is registered inside the `__main__` guard and prod runs gunicorn, so `/utxo/*` is 404 there today. This is latent, not live, and worth fixing before it goes live.

Touches wallet/UTXO code, so the merge decision is Scott's. No overlap with #8268. Suggested tier: standard.

payload.title: fix(tools): fail node sync validator on attention

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Reviewed the real diff (`pulls/8269/files`) and ran the suite locally on the PR head: `tests/test_node_sync_validator.py` -> 15 passed. The change is confined to `tools/node_sync_validator.py` plus tests; no node/consensus code. payload.title: fix(attestation): harden legacy hardware binding

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Reviewed the real diff and the call path on `main`, and reproduced both directions locally.

**Confirmed real.** On `main`, `_check_hardware_binding()` (node file ~L5607) does SELECT-then-INSERT with the insert race swallowed by a bare `except: pass` that still returns `(True, 'Hardware bound', miner_id)`. Your `tests/test_legacy_hardware_binding_race.py` fails on `main` (3 failed: race admits both wallets, spoofed `cpu_serial` mints a fresh binding, locked DB is treated as accepted) and passes on the PR head (69 passed, 18 skipped across the attestation regression files). The `cpu_serial` removal is the more important half: on `main` a client can change one self-reported string and get a brand-new `hardware_id`, which is a one-machine-one-wallet bypass in the legacy path. The path is reachable: `_submit_attestation_impl` falls through to it for any miner not sending `serial`/`serial_number` (~L6045).

**Two things for the maintainer before merge (not blockers for the design, but they change what deploy looks like):**

1. Dropping `cpu_serial` from `hw_fields` changes the hash for every existing row in `hardware_bindings`. After deploy, each legacy miner silently gets a fresh binding on its first attestation and the old row becomes an orphan. That is not a lockout, but it does mean the first wallet to attest from a machine after deploy wins the new binding. Worth a one-line note in the PR body, and ideally a follow-up that garbage-collects rows whose `hardware_id` can no longer be produced.
2. Fail-closed 503 on `sqlite3.Error` is the correct security posture, but it flips the failure mode under lock contention from "silently accept" to "reject attestation". `timeout=10` on the connect makes this unlikely to fire in practice; just flagging so the deploy is watched.

Scope note: production runs a mix of file vintages, so a fix on `main` is not automatically a fix on the node. Deploy is a separate step.

This touches attestation, so the merge decision is Scott's. My read: the fix is correct and the tests are honest. Suggested tier: standard.

payload.author: Vyacheslav-Tomashevskiy
payload.title: fix(hardware-db): substring fallback must anchor to the family minimum, not whichever key matched

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Thanks for this one — the SPARC-T diagnosis is right, and the test does fail on main (3/4) and pass with the patch. But the fix reaches far past SPARC, because the anchoring keys on `entry.family`, and four of the seven databases use a single family label for every row.

I diffed `lookup_hardware()` on main vs this branch for probes that go through the substring fallback:

| probe | family | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `486dx2_66` | x86 | Intel 486 **3.8x** | Core Broadwell **0.8x** |
| `pentium_4_northwood` | x86 | Intel Pentium 3.5x | Core Broadwell 0.8x |
| `core2duo_e8400` | x86 | Core 2 1.5x | Core Broadwell 0.8x |
| `powerbook_g4_titanium` | powerpc | PowerPC G4 2.5x | PowerPC 970 (G5) 2.0x |
| `g4_7447a` | powerpc | PowerPC 7447 2.5x | G5 2.0x |
| `strongarm_sa110` | arm | StrongARM 3.0x | Cortex-A72 0.8x |
| `mc68040_25` | m68k | 68040 3.8x | ColdFire 3.5x |
| `SPARC-T` | sparc | SPARC 3.0x | UltraSPARC III 2.5x (intended) |

Family min/max per DB: x86 `(0.8, 4.0)`, powerpc `(2.0, 4.0)`, arm `(0.8, 4.0)`, m68k `(3.5, 4.0)`. Only `WORKSTATION_DATABASE` has fine-grained families (sparc/alpha/mips/…), which is why the SPARC test alone can't see this.

Suggested shape: the problem is the *generic* root key (`sparc`) winning over the probe's generation, not substring matching itself. Anchor conservatively only when every candidate is a bare family root (or the probe has no generation suffix the DB knows), and otherwise keep the most specific match (longest key). Adding one x86 and one powerpc case from the table above to the test would lock that in.

Blast radius note for the record: nothing outside this module imports `lookup_hardware`/`calculate_poa_multiplier` on main (rip0202 has its own weight table), so this isn't live in settlement today — but it's the reference table people read.

Verified on a main overlay: the PoC fails 3/5 on main (`no such column: miner_id`) and passes 5/5 with the patch. The schema-probe helpers mirror `governance.py` and the unit conversion (`/ LOCK_UNIT` on write, `round(... * LOCK_UNIT)` on read) is consistent.

The part I want to call out, because the title undersells it: the `bridge_transfer_id is not None` refusal in `release_lock()` and the skip in `auto_release_expired_locks()` are a separate, real fix. I checked `bridge_api.py` — `void_bridge_transfer()` updates `lock_ledger` rows itself and tracks the refund on `bridge_transfers.source_debited`; it never calls `release_lock()`. So the expiry worker crediting a bridge-owned lock *would* have double-refunded a deposit. Good catch; please mention it in the PR body so the changelog carries it.

One mechanical thing: the test lives at `node/test_lock_ledger_balance_schema_poc.py` and does a bare `import lock_ledger`, so it only collects when run from inside `node/` (from the repo root it errors at import). Moving it under `node/tests/` with the same `sys.path` prelude your other PoCs use would let CI pick it up.

Bridge balances are money; handing the merge to Scott with a positive read.

payload.body:
Ran this against a main overlay: `node/tests/test_airdrop_concurrent_claim_race.py` 8/8 pass with the patch, 5/8 fail on unmodified main (the three barrier races plus both raw-INSERT index checks). The call path checks out: `claim_airdrop()` now takes `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` before the re-check, the re-check runs on the *same* connection (`_has_claimed_on`), and the partial unique indexes on `(chain, github_username)` / `(chain, wallet_address)` filtered to pending/completed are the correct expression of the rule `_has_claimed()` always intended. The legacy-duplicates path logging instead of refusing to boot is the right failure mode.

Two small things, neither blocking:
- `_normalize_wallet_address` lowercases Base addresses at claim time. Worth a one-liner in the description that this is also a (good) behaviour change for `check_eligibility`, since anyone reading claim rows for Base will now see lowercase.
- The `finally: conn.isolation_level = prev_isolation` restore is nice; consider a comment that `_get_conn()` hands out a fresh connection per call so the manual-isolation toggle can't leak across callers.

Airdrop allocation is money, so the merge decision is Scott's — flagging it to him as verified and ready.

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
⛔ **Hold this PR — do not merge yet.** A private security review (verified from source with a passing network-free repro today) found that moving the UTXO blueprint registration to module level, which this PR does, makes `/utxo/transfer` reachable under gunicorn — and that endpoint currently has a **confirmed double-spend** under a dual-write ON→OFF cycle: its dual-write branch mints receiver+change boxes with no `account_mirror_boxes` provenance, so after a rollback to `UTXO_DUAL_WRITE=0` the same value is spendable through both the UTXO and account models, while the total-only `integrity_check` still reports `models_agree=True`. It's the residual the #2819 fix did not close (that covered the account→UTXO direction; this is UTXO→account).

Today it's latent only because `/utxo/*` 404s under gunicorn — which is exactly what this PR changes. So the registration move must ship **with** the fix, not before it. Minimal fix: drop the `if not _dual_write:` guard at `utxo_endpoints.py:713` and `:800` so migrated mirror boxes always move via the account path in both configs; independently add a per-wallet `mirror <= balance` assertion to `integrity_check` so a divergence can't hide behind matching totals. Happy to fold that into this branch. The rewards/RIP-201 fixes in here are still good and wanted.

payload.title: [Bounty Hunter Bot] Fix broken links in README.md (bounty #16248)

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Checked each of the three claims:

1. `Rustchain` → `RustChain`: GitHub repository URLs are case-insensitive, and `/stargazers` returns 404 to anonymous fetches under *both* spellings (verified today). The capitalisation change doesn't fix anything; the working fix (#8197, now merged) points the link at the repo root.
2. DOI swap `zenodo.20502069` → `zenodo.19442753`: both records resolve fine in a browser (Zenodo returns 403 to non-browser HEAD requests, which is what your check saw). More importantly they are different papers — 20502069 is *RIP-0310 Proof of Provenance*, which is what that paragraph is about; 19442753 is *RIP-0308 Proof of Physical AI*. The change would make the README cite the wrong paper.
3. DexScreener: no change.

So the net effect of the diff is one cosmetic change and one factual error. Closing this out as not mergeable; the bounty itself (#16248) was delivered and paid via #8019 in July.

payload.author: marcusdytrich
payload.body:
I tested the tutorial's Quick Start commands against the current base (`main` at `1f5db5df13ea84c91ab048e7382bb7625840071f`) and found three reproducible onboarding blockers that should be corrected before merge:

1. **Python miner command points to a file that does not exist.** The tutorial tells readers to run `python miner.py --wallet YOUR_WALLET_ADDRESS`, but there is no root `miner.py`. The current Linux miner is `miners/linux/rustchain_linux_miner.py` (and platform-specific miners live under `miners/`). A fresh user following the tutorial stops here with file-not-found.

2. **Rust build command is run from the wrong directory.** The tutorial says `cargo build --release` from the repository root, but current `main` has no root `Cargo.toml`. The Rust wallet is under `rustchain-wallet/`; other Rust components need their own crate directory. Please make the exact supported miner crate/path explicit rather than giving a root build command that cannot run.

3. **Epoch monitoring endpoint is stale.** `curl https://rustchain.org/api/epoch` currently returns HTTP 404, while `https://rustchain.org/epoch` returns HTTP 200. The monitoring example should use the live route.

Verification performed locally against the exact current base: `requirements.txt` exists; `miner.py` does not; root `Cargo.toml` does not; `miners/linux/rustchain_linux_miner.py` exists; live probes returned `/api/epoch -> 404` and `/epoch -> 200`. payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.title: fix(ci,monitoring): three guards that could not report a failure

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
### Update: the first CI run of this branch immediately found a real bug

The new failure path did its job on its very first run, and caught something `continue-on-error: true` had been swallowing.

The live node answers `/api/miners` with a JSON list of miner-id **strings**, not objects. So `m.get("antiquity_multiplier", 1.0)` raised `AttributeError` partway through `live_api_checks` — *after* `node_health`, `epoch_consistency`, and `epoch_pot` had already passed:

```
[3/3] Live node API invariant checks...
  ✅ LIVE node_health
  ✅ LIVE epoch_consistency (epoch=259)
  ✅ LIVE epoch_pot=1.5 RTC
AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'
```

That crash has presumably been happening on every run of this workflow, invisibly, for as long as `continue-on-error: true` was there. **The live invariant checks past `epoch_pot` — the antiquity-multiplier and total-balance checks — have never actually run against production.**

But my first pass reported it as **exit 1, "the live chain violated a ledger invariant"** — which is wrong in the opposite direction from the bug this PR exists to fix. A crash in the checker is not a verdict about the chain.

Fixed in `cfa8af9`:

1. **Validate payload shape before indexing into it.** `/api/miners` that isn't a list of objects, `/epoch` or `/api/stats` that isn't an object, and a non-numeric `total_balance` are now recorded as UNMEASURED, with the observed type and a sample value:
   ```
   UNMEASURED /api/miners: 3/3 entries are not objects (first is str: 'dual-g4-125');
   antiquity multipliers cannot be read from this shape
   ```
2. **A checker crash gets its own exit code (3).** `live_api_checks` is wrapped; an unexpected exception is recorded as `checker_error`, prints its traceback, and exits 3 under its own annotation. It still fails the run — a guard that cannot run is a broken guard — but it is no longer announced as a chain violation. `summary.all_invariants_hold` is `None`, never `True`, when the checker crashed.

Re-verified against a local server reproducing the exact live shape from the failing run (no production host contacted):

| scenario | exit | result |
|---|---|---|
| healthy | `0` | ALL INVARIANTS HOLD |
| **the real live shape** (`/api/miners` = list of strings) | `2` | 1 check unmeasured, 0 violations, **no crash** |
| `epoch_pot=2.75` | `1` | `LIVE VIOLATION [epoch_pot]` |
| SPA answering 200-with-HTML | `2` | 4 checks unmeasured |
| forced `AttributeError` | `3` | "the CHECKER crashed", not a violation |

**Worth a maintainer's judgement:** the miners check is now correctly reported as *unmeasured* rather than passing, which is honest but means it still isn't checking anything on production. Whether the right follow-up is to teach the checker the node's actual `/api/miners` schema, or to change the endpoint, is a call I shouldn't make unilaterally — but it should not stay unmeasured indefinitely.

**Still not verified:** the workflow's `case "$rc"` branch for exit 3 has not been observed in a CI run.

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
### Correction and follow-up: the miners invariant now actually runs

Two things from the CI runs.

**1. My description of the bug was slightly wrong.** I said `/api/miners` returns "a list of strings". It returns a JSON **object** — an envelope. Iterating it yielded the dict's *keys*, which are strings, and that is where `'str' object has no attribute 'get'` came from. Same crash, more precise cause.

**2. Reporting it as UNMEASURED wasn't good enough.** `cfa8af9` correctly stopped the crash, but left the antiquity-multiplier and ordering invariants permanently unmeasured on production. Honest — but "unmeasured forever" quietly becomes the same blind spot the tolerated crash was, which is the exact failure mode this PR is about.

`4b05128` unwraps the envelope using the same `miners` / `data` / `items` key order that `tools/rustchain-health.py` already uses, so both readers in this repo agree on the schema. An object with none of those keys, or a list whose entries aren't objects, is still reported UNMEASURED with the observed shape.

### Result on the live chain

```
[3/3] Live node API invariant checks...
  ✅ LIVE node_health
  ✅ LIVE epoch_consistency (epoch=259)
  ✅ LIVE epoch_pot=1.5 RTC
  ✅ LIVE miner_multipliers (15 miners, all >= 0)
  ✅ LIVE antiquity_ordering
  ✅ LIVE total_balance >= 0 (453154.6859 RTC)

✅ ALL INVARIANTS HOLD — RustChain ledger math is correct
```

`Ledger Invariant Test Suite  pass`

**`miner_multipliers` and `antiquity_ordering` are running against production for the first time.** They were unreachable behind the `AttributeError` for as long as `continue-on-error: true` was masking it, and the run was green throughout.

So the progression across this branch, all observed in CI rather than asserted:

| commit | outcome | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `eef3e03` | **fail**, exit 1 | crash surfaced, but mislabelled as a chain violation |
| `cfa8af9` | pass + `::warning` | crash classified as UNMEASURED — honest, still no coverage |
| `4b05128` | **pass**, all 6 measured | real coverage, legitimately green |

### Now verified in CI (updating my earlier "not verified")

- The workflow runs, and its `case "$rc"` branching works for exit `1` (failed the run with the violation annotation) and exit `2` (passed with `::warning title=Live node unmeasurable`).
- `[report] wrote JSON report to ledger_invariants_report.json`, and the "Verify report is valid JSON" step passes.
- The widened `paths` trigger fires.

### Still not verified

- The exit-`3` branch (checker crash) has not occurred in CI. It was exercised locally by forcing an exception into `live_api_checks`.
- Nothing here proves the invariants are *correct*, only that they now run and that a violation reddens the build. The synthetic `epoch_pot=2.75` case confirms the failure path end to end; a real violation on production has not been observed, which is the desired state.

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
## Update: lever B is now in this PR

Pushed `64e7007b`, which connects the temporal consistency score to the reward. All checks green.

**The node already remembered, and then ignored the memory.** `validate_temporal_consistency` has been scoring every miner against its own past measurements for months, and it already detects the two shapes a forged history takes:

| flag | condition | what it catches |
|---|---|---|
| `frozen_profile` | `rel_var < 0.01` | the same value replayed every epoch |
| `noisy_profile` | `rel_var > 0.8` | an RNG with no physical model behind it |

Its only consumer was `app.logger.warning(...)`. A miner contradicting its own history collected the full antiquity premium anyway.

The score now gates the bonus:

```
effective = 1.0 + (hw_weight - 1.0) * score
```

Only weight **above baseline** is at risk. A modern miner at 0.8x is untouched, and nobody is pushed below the baseline every participant already earns, so a false positive costs a premium rather than someone's participation. The premium is also the only thing on this chain worth forging, which is why it is the only thing gated.

**Cold start is inverted.** Insufficient history used to return `score: 1.0`, so a brand new identity — the cheapest thing a forger can make — was the most trusted thing on the chain. It now receives half the bonus: not zero, which would punish honest newcomers, and not one, which made a fresh identity the cheapest route to the premium. `TEMPORAL_UNVERIFIED_BONUS_FRACTION` is named and commented as a tokenomics knob rather than buried as a literal.

**This is not a tenure multiplier and must not become one.** Nothing here pays for age. History length only decides whether there is enough observation to check a claim. What earns the bonus is staying *consistent*, and that is the property a farm cannot mass-produce: every identity must be self-consistent across time **and** independent of the others, and those two constraints pull against each other. A shared generator leaves cross-identity correlation; avoiding it means modelling each fake machine separately. Tenure had neither property, which is why it was rejected 5/5 as software-cheap.

Applied on **both** weight paths. Enrollment is what actually sets epoch weight, so gating attestation alone would have been cosmetic, and a test asserts both call sites exist by walking the AST. That test exists because the failure being fixed here is precisely "correct helper, nobody calls it" — a unit test on the helper alone would have passed the whole time it was broken.

### One existing assertion changed

`test_legacy_miner_without_verified_device_falls_back_to_body` asserted exact equality with the body-declared weight. A legacy row with no verified device, claiming ARM `arm2` at 4.0x **from the unsigned request body**, now receives 2.5.

Its documented promise was *"not regressed to weight 1.0"*, and that still holds. The exact-equality assertion was stricter than the promise it stated. This is the least-evidenced weight on the chain and it was collecting the largest multiplier available.

### Verification

- 13 new tests, including a false-positive guard: an honest G4 whose readings wander a few percent keeps its full 2.5x. Without that guard this control would repeat the mistake it exists to fix, firing only on honest miners.
- `tests/`: **3757 passed, 0 failed**
- `node/tests/`: diffed against clean `main` — **no new failures, three fixed**
- `ruff` clean on the new file; baseline unchanged elsewhere

### Still open

Freshness binding. `derive_measurement_nonce` is computed, stored and logged, but **never verified**, and no client in `miners/` reads it — so nothing binds a measurement to a time window and a payload measured once can be replayed forever. Consistency scoring raises the cost of a forged history; it does not yet force the forger to execute per epoch. That needs client changes, so it is deliberately not in this PR.

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Reviewed properly. **The fix is correct** — and I am still not merging it myself. Both halves of that need explaining.

### The bug is real, and worse than the title suggests

Pre-fix, `_determine_tier` called `GET /search/commits` with `q="author:{user} merged:true"`. Two independent problems:

1. `merged:true` **is not a qualifier the commit-search index supports** — it is an issue/PR qualifier. GitHub does not error on an unknown qualifier there; it folds it into free text. So the count coming back was never "merged PRs."
2. Even had it worked, `search/commits` is **global** — every commit the user ever authored anywhere on GitHub. Airdrop tier was being set by a stranger's unrelated open-source history rather than by contribution to this project.

Moving to `search/issues` with `author:{user} org:Scottcjn is:pr is:merged` fixes both. The comment you replaced the old one with — "Count merged PRs scoped to the RustChain org, not global GitHub activity" — is an accurate description of what the code now does, which is not something I take for granted.

### What I verified rather than assumed

`Scottcjn` is a **User** account, not an Organization (`GET /users/Scottcjn` → `"type": "User"`), so I specifically checked whether the `org:` qualifier silently returns nothing against a user account — which would have turned every applicant into a Stargazer. It does not; GitHub resolves `org:` against user accounts too. Live check:

```
q=author:Vyacheslav-Tomashevskiy org:Scottcjn is:pr is:merged   → total_count 184
q=author:Vyacheslav-Tomashevskiy user:Scottcjn is:pr is:merged  → total_count 184
```

Identical. The qualifier choice is safe. I would still mildly prefer `user:` as the more literally-correct form, but that is taste, not a defect, and I am not going to hold the PR for it.

Also dropping the `cloak-preview` Accept header along with `search/commits` is right — that preview only ever applied to commit search.

### Why this is not merging on my say-so

This changes **who gets how much RTC**. Airdrop tier determination is reward-issuing logic on a production chain, and our standing rule is that a reviewer in my position does not merge reward, consensus, wallet, attestation, or settlement code on their own authority no matter how clean it reads. So:

**BLOCKED-for-human — needs @Scottcjn.** This is a queue-position problem, not a quality problem. The technical review above is a recommendation to merge.

One thing for whoever picks this up, because it is a genuine decision and not a nit: this fix **changes existing users' tiers**. Anyone previously tiered on inflated global commit counts will re-tier lower on their next evaluation. Whether already-issued airdrops get honored or recalculated is a policy call that should be made deliberately, not discovered after the fact.

Your test asserting the exact query string is the right shape for this — it pins the scoping so a future refactor cannot quietly widen it again. Thanks for catching this one.

payload.title: fix(security): reject unsigned attestations in /attest/submit (fixes #8178) [fj4WqyCCw3C5ShR1RfB7MoBPTpkRrBFYP1uT35g3MvT]

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Thanks for the write-up on #8178 — the concern was correct, and I want to be clear that it has already been addressed on `main`, which is why this can't merge as written.

**What main has now** (`node/rustchain_v2_integrated_v2.2.1_rip200.py`, ~5728–5800, landed via #8016):

- `INCOMPLETE_SIGNATURE` 400 for a lone signature/public_key — always on, exactly what your first hunk adds.
- A phased gate `RTC_ATTEST_ENFORCE_MODE = log_only | enforce_new | enforce_all` (`_attest_enforce_mode`, line 354): new identities must sign in Phase 1, everyone in Phase 2, with an operator allowlist for hardware that structurally can't sign and a grandfather table for existing miners.

**Why merging this would regress**

The unconditional `SIGNED_ATTESTATION_REQUIRED` 401 in your second hunk sits *before* that gate and ignores both the allowlist and grandfathering. In practice it would kick the legacy PowerPC miners (Python 2.x-era clients with no PyNaCl) off the network in one deploy, which is the outcome the phased rollout exists to avoid. The branch also conflicts with `main`, since the hunk is against an older layout of `_submit_attestation_impl`.

**Something that would be useful**

`unsigned_attestation_poc.py` is nicely structured. If you re-point it at the existing gate as a regression test — assert 400 `MISSING_SIGNATURE` for a new unsigned identity under `enforce_new`, 400 `INCOMPLETE_SIGNATURE` for a partial pair, and acceptance for a grandfathered/allowlisted miner — that would be a genuine addition and I'd review it quickly.

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Holding this, and I want to be clear that the vulnerability is real. Accepting an attestation with no signature and no public key means no proof that the submitter controls the wallet, which is a Sybil vector rather than a theoretical one. It should be closed.

**It cannot be closed as a hard cutover, though.** As written this returns 401 for every attestation without `signature` and `public_key`, and the live fleet does not send them.

What I checked:

- The code path you are removing is a documented compatibility path. The comment directly above it at line 5039 reads: *"Operators who intentionally run without pynacl can still accept unsigned attestations via the backward-compat path below (no signature fields, no verification attempted)."* So unsigned is the currently supported case, not an oversight.
- No current miner client sends those fields. Grepping `miners/` for `"signature"` and `public_key` outside `deprecated/old_miners/` returns nothing.
- The node has 15 miners attesting right now, including PowerPC G4 and G5 machines on very old Python where adding Ed25519 signing is not a small change.

So merging this stops attestation for the entire fleet at once, and the vintage hardware is exactly the part that is hardest to upgrade. That is a chain halt for the miners rather than a hardening.

**A migration that gets you the same end state:**

1. Land the signature verification path and keep unsigned accepted, but mark unsigned attestations in the database and log them, so there is a real count of who still needs upgrading.
2. Ship signing in the miner clients, and confirm from that count that the fleet has moved over. The vintage miners will need the most lead time.
3. Gate enforcement behind a flag, defaulting to permissive, so the cutover is an operator decision and is reversible without a redeploy. The existing `RC_TESTNET_ALLOW_MOCK_SIG` and `RC_TESTNET_ALLOW_INLINE_PUBKEY` environment switches are the established pattern.
4. Flip the default once the count reaches zero.

Step 1 alone is a genuinely useful PR and I would take it now.

Two smaller notes:

- `unsigned_attestation_poc.py` is added at the repository root. PoC files belong beside the tests rather than at top level, and this repo has a pattern of PoC tests that assert the bug is present, which then fail once it is fixed. Worth writing it as a test that asserts the *fixed* behaviour instead.
- The `elif sig_hex or pubkey_hex` branch rejecting a half-supplied pair with 400 is correct and uncontroversial. That part could go in on its own immediately.

The finding is good work. It is the rollout that needs to change, not the analysis.

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Follow-up that should save you a lot of work: **the staged migration this PR needs already exists on the production node**, it just never made it back to `main`.

The live node at 50.28.86.131 carries seven functions that main does not have, all wired:

```
RTC_ATTEST_ENFORCE_MODE:
  log_only     (Phase 0, DEFAULT)  verify signatures if present, enforce nothing
  enforce_new  (Phase 1)           new identities must sign; grandfathered stay unsigned
  enforce_all  (Phase 2)           every miner must present a valid signature
```

plus `_attest_unsigned_allowlist()`, a grandfather table, and an `admin_attest_key` endpoint.

That is precisely the rollout I described in my earlier review: enforcement behind a flag, defaulting permissive, with grandfathering so the vintage fleet is not cut off mid-upgrade. Someone built it properly and it was left behind on the box.

So the useful shape for this PR is not the hard 401. It is:

1. port those functions from the production file into `main` (they are the missing half of the signed-attestation story), then
2. wire `/attest/submit` to consult `_attest_enforce_mode()` rather than rejecting unconditionally.

Under `log_only` nothing changes for anyone, which makes the change safe to merge immediately, and the cutover later becomes an env var rather than a redeploy.

Your finding was right, and it is worth more than the diff suggested: an unsigned attestation genuinely proves no wallet ownership. It is the rollout that needed to change, and it turns out the rollout was already designed.

payload.title: fix: require X-P2P-Key auth on /p2p/gossip POST endpoint (fixes #8177) [fj4WqyCCw3C5ShR1RfB7MoBPTpkRrBFYP1uT35g3MvT]

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Holding this one, and I want to be precise about why, because the finding behind it is correct.

You are right that `/p2p/gossip` POST is the odd one out. `_require_p2p_read_auth()` already exists at line 1811 and guards the sensitive read-only sync endpoints, and the sender at line 1538 already sends `X-P2P-Key`. The gossip receive path having no auth is a genuine gap.

**The problem is the other sender.** `broadcast()` at line 884 is the live fan-out path, and it goes through `_send_to_peer()` at line 894:

```python
def _send_to_peer(self, peer_url: str, msg: GossipMessage):
    resp = requests.post(
        f"{peer_url}/p2p/gossip",
        json=msg.to_dict(),
        timeout=10,
        verify=TLS_VERIFY
    )
```

No `X-P2P-Key` header. This diff adds the header to zero senders (`git diff origin/main...HEAD | grep -c X-P2P-Key` returns 0), so as soon as the receiving side requires the key, **every gossip message from `broadcast()` gets a 401 and inter-node gossip stops**. That is a fleet-wide outage rather than a hardening.

CI does not catch it: this needs two nodes talking to each other, and nothing in the suite exercises that. The branch is green and mergeable, which is exactly why I checked the call path by hand.

**What would make this mergeable:**

1. Add the header in `_send_to_peer()`, matching line 1538:
   ```python
   headers={"X-P2P-Key": P2P_SECRET},
   ```
2. Consider the rollout order explicitly. If receivers start requiring the key before every peer is running a sender that sends it, older peers get cut off mid-upgrade. Enforcing on receive only when `P2P_SECRET` is configured, or logging-and-allowing for one release before enforcing, avoids a hard cutover. Your call which, but the PR should say which it assumes.
3. A test that a gossip POST without the header is rejected and one with it is accepted, since there is no coverage of this path at all right now.

Worth flagging separately: this branch is also stacked under #8191 and #8192, so each of those carries this change plus its own. If this one needs a revision, they inherit it. Splitting them onto independent branches off current `main` would make all three reviewable on their own merits.

The gap you found is real and worth fixing. It just needs the sender side to land in the same change.

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Follow-up: the sender half is now on `main`.

#8203 adds `X-P2P-Key` to `_send_to_peer()`, so both gossip senders present the key. It is inert on its own, because `/p2p/gossip` still does not require it, and it ships an AST-based test asserting every `requests.post` to that endpoint passes the header, so a future sender added without it fails in CI instead of in production.

That removes the outage risk from your change. Rebase onto current `main` and this becomes mergeable on its own merits.

One thing still worth deciding in your PR: the rollout order. Even with every sender fixed, a receiver that starts enforcing before all peers are running the new build will cut off the stragglers. Gating enforcement on an env flag, defaulting permissive, makes the cutover an operator decision and reversible without a redeploy. `RC_TESTNET_ALLOW_MOCK_SIG` is the established pattern in this codebase.

Thanks for finding the gap.

payload.author: waterWang
payload.title: fix: wrap mempool_clear_expired() in BEGIN IMMEDIATE to prevent concurrent mempool corruption (fixes #8176) [fj4WqyCCw3C5ShR1RfB7MoBPTpkRrBFYP1uT35g3MvT]

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Verified and merging. Checked out the branch, merged current `main` into it (clean, no conflicts), and ran the suites:

- `test_utxo_db` 103 passed
- `test_utxo_endpoints` + `test_rollback_atomicity` 48 passed
- `test_utxo_security_audit` 24 passed
- the UTXO #2819 regression suite merged earlier today, 7 passed
- `check_fetchall.sh` clean

The claim holds on `main`: `mempool_clear_expired()` did a SELECT, then two DELETEs per row, then `commit()`, with no write lock across the sequence, while `mempool_remove()` right below it documents using `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` for exactly that reason. Matching the two is the right call.

I also checked the nesting risk, since wrapping a method in `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` breaks if a caller already holds a transaction. Both call sites, `mempool_add()` at line 1188 and `mempool_get_block_candidates()` at 1506, invoke it before opening their own transaction and on a separate connection, so there is no nested-transaction path.

One thing for you to know, since it is a consequence of your fix rather than a defect in it: `node/test_utxo_mempool_concurrent_stress_poc.py` is written to *confirm the vulnerability*, asserting that `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` is absent. It passes on `main` and fails on your branch, precisely because you fixed the thing it asserts. CI does not catch this, as the `test` job runs `pytest tests/` and that PoC lives in `node/`. I am converting it into a regression test in a follow-up so it now asserts the lock is present. No action needed from you.

Thank you for the fix.

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Reviewed. Two things here, and the second one matters more than the first.

## 1. The branch carries more than the title says

Title: *"fix(wallet): consistent error handling + exit codes for balance check"*. Actual file list:

```
23+  7-  rip302_agent_economy.py
254+ 0-  tests/test_agent_dispute_redelivery.py
19+  5-  wallet/coinbase_wallet.py
163+ 0-  wallet/tests/test_wallet_balance_error_handling.py
```

The first two files are **PR #8086 in its entirety** — the RIP-302 disputed-job re-delivery fix, byte-identical. That is escrow logic riding under a wallet-CLI title.

I do not read this as anything but branch stacking after the backlog pass moved `main` under everyone. But it has to be fixed before merge, because a human skimming "wallet exit codes" would not expect to be approving changes to job escrow state transitions. Please rebase this branch onto current `main` so it contains **only** the two `wallet/` files, and let #8086 carry the RIP-302 change on its own. I have reviewed #8086 separately on its merits — it is sound.

## 2. A real defect in the wallet change: the diagnostic is split across two streams

The change moves *some* error output to stderr and leaves the rest on stdout, in both error paths.

No-wallet path:
```python
print(f"\n  {YELLOW}No Coinbase wallet found.{NC}")                              # stdout
print(f"  Create one: clawrtc wallet coinbase create")                          # stdout
print(f"  Or link:    clawrtc wallet coinbase link 0xYourAddress\n", file=sys.stderr)   # stderr
sys.exit(1)
```

Balance-fetch path:
```python
print(f"  {RED}Error: Unable to fetch balance{NC}", file=sys.stderr)            # stderr
print(f"    {error}", file=sys.stderr)                                          # stderr
print(f"  {DIM}Troubleshooting:{NC}")                                           # stdout
print(f"    - Verify internet access and DNS resolution")                       # stdout
print(f"    - Check RustChain node availability at {NODE_URL}", file=sys.stderr)  # stderr
```

In the second case the troubleshooting block is torn in half — its header and first bullet go to stdout, its second bullet to stderr. Anyone doing the thing exit codes exist for, `clawrtc wallet coinbase show 2>/dev/null` or `... >out.txt`, gets a fragment of a message either way: a bare "Troubleshooting:" header with one orphan bullet, or two bullets with no header.

Set against the PR title — *"**consistent** error handling"* — and the new docstring that presents a clean four-code contract, this is the docstring-stricter-than-code pattern. The contract described is tidy; the stream routing under it is not. Fix is mechanical: every line of an error diagnostic goes to stderr, full stop, in both paths.

## 3. Smaller notes, not blockers

- **`sys.exit(0)` at the end of `coinbase_show`.** `coinbase_show` is a dispatch-table handler (`dispatch["show"]`, called via `func(args)` in `cmd_coinbase`), not a `main()`. Exiting the process from inside a subcommand handler makes the function unusable in-process and means any future caller that wants to do work after `show` cannot. Returning `0` and letting the CLI entry point exit is the cleaner shape. Harmless today; a trap later.
- **Exit-code 2-vs-3 keys off substring matching** on the error text (`"Network unreachable" in error or "Request failed" in error`). That silently reclassifies network failures as code 3 the day someone rewords a message in `_get_wallet_balance_from_node`. A small enum or error type at the source would make the documented contract actually enforceable. The docstring promises a stable meaning for 2 and 3 that string-matching cannot guarantee.

## Decision

**BLOCKED-for-human — needs @Scottcjn**, and needs a rebase from you first.

Concretely, the fastest path:
1. Rebase this branch onto current `main` so it holds only `wallet/coinbase_wallet.py` + `wallet/tests/test_wallet_balance_error_handling.py`.
2. Route the whole diagnostic to stderr in both paths.
3. Drop t

payload.title: fix(security): enforce Ed25519 verification and hide escrow_secret (#8179)

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Thanks for picking up #8179 — the intent (authenticate `from_wallet`, don't leak secrets) is right. Three things in the implementation would break the escrow system in production, so I'm requesting changes rather than merging.

**1. `result.pop("escrow_secret", None)` permanently locks every escrow**

In `node/gpu_render_protocol.py` the secret is generated once in `create_escrow` (line 293), only its hash is persisted (line 302), and the create response (line 313) is the *single* place the plaintext is ever handed to the caller. `release_escrow` (318) and `refund_escrow` (360) both go through `_authorize_escrow_action` (160–171), which requires the plaintext and compares against the stored hash. With the plaintext removed from the create response, no party can ever release or refund — the RTC is locked with no recovery path. The secret is a show-once bearer capability by design; the fix for "leakage" is to make sure it never appears in *list/get* responses, not to strip it from create.

**2. `bytes.fromhex(from_wallet)` rejects every legitimate caller**

`from_wallet` is a wallet identifier (`founder_team_bounty`, `gpu-farm-rack3`, an `RTC…`-prefixed address), not a raw Ed25519 public key. `bytes.fromhex` raises on all of these, the broad `except Exception` catches it, and every `create_escrow` returns 401. The node's existing convention (see `/wallet/transfer/signed`) is a separate `public_key` field with the address derived from it — that's the pattern to reuse here. Also worth binding the signed `message` to `to_wallet`/`amount_rtc`/a nonce; as written a captured signature can be replayed to open escrows from that wallet indefinitely.

**3. The airdrop half fails open**

`github_token` is `Optional[str] = None` in `claim_airdrop` (line 778) and the new check is wrapped in `if github_token:`. A caller who simply omits the token skips verification entirely, which is the exact bypass the check exists to close. Make the token required (or reject when absent).

The new tests exercise the code as written, so they pass — but they don't exercise a release after a create, which is where (1) shows up. A test that creates then releases would catch it.

The branch also conflicts with `main` now. If you rework along the lines above (pubkey field + bound message, keep the secret in the create response only, mandatory token) I'd be glad to re-review.

payload.title: [UTXO-BUG] Reject non-finite JSON output metadata

payload.author: lequangsang01
payload.body:
## Code Review: Reject non-finite JSON output metadata (UTXO-BUG)

### Summary
Python's built-in `json.loads` by default accepts non-standard IEEE 754 float constants (`NaN`, `Infinity`, `-Infinity`), which are invalid under standard RFC 8259 JSON and cause parsing crashes across Rust/Go/Node.js miners/nodes. This PR rejects non-finite constants at the `_normalize_outputs` layer in `node/utxo_db.py` using `parse_constant`.

### Line-Level Analysis

**1. `node/utxo_db.py:124-126` — `_reject_nonstandard_json_constant`**
```python
def _reject_nonstandard_json_constant(value: str):
    """Reject Python's non-standard NaN/Infinity JSON extensions."""
    raise ValueError(f"non-standard JSON constant: {value}")
```
- **Analysis:** Raising `ValueError` on `NaN` / `Infinity` correctly triggers the existing `except (TypeError, ValueError):` handler in `_normalize_outputs`, causing `_normalize_outputs` to return `None` and cleanly reject invalid transaction outputs without throwing an unhandled exception.

**2. `node/utxo_db.py:586-591` — `parse_constant` hook in `json.loads`**
```python
tokens = json.loads(tokens_json, parse_constant=_reject_nonstandard_json_constant)
registers = json.loads(registers_json, parse_constant=_reject_nonstandard_json_constant)
```
- **Analysis:** Prevents mempool poisoning where an attacker submits malformed `tokens_json` or `registers_json` containing `[NaN]` or `{"R4": -Infinity}`.

**3. `node/test_utxo_db.py:1803-1858` — Unit Test Coverage**
- Tests both `mempool_add` (verifying input box is NOT double-spend locked on rejection) and `apply_transaction` (verifying state rollbacks correctly).

### Verdict & Security Assessment
✅ **LGTM** — Clean, line-level security fix that enforces RFC 8259 JSON compliance and prevents cross-language UTXO deserialization consensus failures.

**Wallet:** `RTCfe13452d122263caf633ab1876bd9631133b68b1`

payload.author: qiann0512-gif
payload.body:
The touch gesture mapping is a useful direction, but the new tap detector still treats the primary finger from a multi-touch gesture as a possible tap. On `pointerdown` the code stores `pointerStart` for the primary touch, and adding a second touch for `TWO = DOLLY_PAN` does not clear or cancel that candidate. When the primary finger lifts, `pointerup` can still run `selectAt(e)` if that finger moved less than 10px, even though the user was performing a two-finger zoom/pan. That can accidentally select an agent/city or fire `onMissHandler()` and close the panel at the end of a pinch gesture, which is exactly the mobile interaction this PR is trying to make safe.

Please track active touch pointers and cancel the pending tap as soon as a second touch pointer enters, or otherwise mark the gesture as dragged/multitouch until all touches end. A focused regression/manual test for two-finger zoom/pan without opening/closing details would make this much safer to merge.

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Re-verified today: the touch mapping (`ONE = ROTATE`, `TWO = DOLLY_PAN`) is right for OrbitControls, and the move from `click` to pointer events also fixes the pre-existing desktop bug where raycast selection used stale coordinates after a drag — a good catch beyond the bounty scope.

The one nit @qiann0512-gif raised is still present in `scene.js`: `pointerdown` records `pointerStart` for the primary finger (line 72), nothing clears it when a second finger arrives, and `pointerup` calls `selectAt(e)` whenever the primary moved under 10px (lines 78–81). A pinch where the primary finger stays roughly in place ends with an accidental select or `onMissHandler()` closing the panel. Small fix: track an active-pointer count (increment on `pointerdown`, decrement on `pointerup`/`pointercancel`) and set `pointerStart = null` whenever the count exceeds one. With that this looks ready to approve.

payload.author: 0wmz
payload.title: feat(tools): agent-to-agent on-chain transfer harness + tests (rustchain-bounties#13519)

payload.author: qiann0512-gif
payload.body:
The signing helpers look aligned with `_wallet_transfer_signed_messages`, but the `roundtrip` orchestration does not match the live `/wallet/transfer/signed` settlement semantics. That endpoint returns `ok: true` when it inserts a `pending_ledger` row and includes `phase: "pending"` plus a delayed `confirms_at`; it does not credit the recipient balance immediately. In this PR, `round_trip()` treats `outbound.ok` as “landed” and immediately tries the B->A return leg.

That means the advertised round-trip only works if agent B was already independently funded before the test. If B is supposed to return the 1 RTC it just received from A, the return leg will still see B's pre-transfer available balance and can fail with insufficient funds until the pending transfer confirms. The README also says the tool writes a complete receipt for A->B then B->A, but the receipt can show a failed inbound leg even though the first leg is merely pending, not settled.

Please either make the round-trip flow wait/poll until the outbound `pending_id` is confirmed before attempting the return transfer, or document and enforce that both agents must already have enough spendable balance for their leg. A regression can fake the node returning `phase: "pending"` on outbound and insufficient balance on immediate inbound to lock this behavior down.

payload.author: lequangsang01
payload.body:
## Code Review: Agent-to-Agent (A2A) On-Chain Transfer Harness & Tests

### Summary
Implements an end-to-end Python harness (`tools/a2a_transfer_harness.py`) and unit test suite (`tests/test_a2a_transfer_harness.py`) for Agent-to-Agent (A2A) on-chain transfers. Covers Ed25519 signing, canonical JSON message serialization with fallback for legacy signatures, monotonic nonces, and double-leg round-trip testing.

### Key Highlights & Line-Level Observations

1. **Canonical Message Serialization & Legacy Fallback:**
   ```python
   current, legacy = a2a.canonical_messages(
       payload["from_address"], payload["to_address"], payload["amount_rtc"],
       payload.get("fee_rtc", 0.0), payload.get("memo", ""), payload["nonce"], payload.get("chain_id")
   )
   ```
   - **Good:** Correctly handles compact JSON encoding (`b', '` / `b': '` omitted) matching the node's `verify_signed_message` specification. The legacy fallback handles node versions prior to `fee_rtc` inclusion without breaking active agents.

2. **Wallet Address Validation:**
   ```python
   ADDRESS_RE = re.compile(r"^RTC[a-f0-9]{40}$")
   ```
   - **Good:** Strict regex enforcement requiring `RTC` prefix followed by exactly 40 lower-case hex characters. Rejects non-native wallet shapes (`0x...`, capital `RTC...`) early before building network payloads.

3. **Self-Transfer & Amount Guards:**
   - Enforces `amount >= 1.0 RTC` (RIP-201 minimum transfer rule) and rejects self-transfers (`from_address == to_address`) to prevent unnecessary gas/nonce burns.

4. **Monotonic Nonce Generator:**
   - `NonceFactory` uses microsecond timestamps paired with strict increment tracking to guarantee nonces remain strictly increasing across rapid sub-second agent transfers.

5. **Test Suite Coverage:**
   - 100% offline test coverage using `httpx.MockTransport` / custom callable openers testing error paths, key loading from hex/json, CLI subcommands, and failed return-leg handling.

payload.title: fix(installer): resolve macOS crashes, missing variables, and sha256 fallback in install.sh

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Closing on security grounds. This PR's sha256 miner-id fallback interpolates `${wallet}` directly into a `python3 -c` string literal:

```bash
miner_id=$(python3 -c "import hashlib; print(hashlib.sha256(b'${wallet}-${arch}-' + b'$(hostname)').hexdigest()[:16])" ...)
```

A crafted `--wallet` value breaks out of the string and executes arbitrary code — e.g. `--wallet "a'+__import__('os').system('...')+'b"` — in an installer that is run as root via `curl | bash`. This replaces `main`'s safe shell pipe (`echo -n ... | sha256sum`, which passes the wallet as data, not code) with an injectable one, so it introduces a root RCE rather than fixing anything. `main` does not currently have this vulnerability.

Two other claims here do not hold up: the cited macOS `MINER_CRYPTO_URL` bug is branch-guarded and never reached on Darwin, and the bash-3.2 / path fixes for issue #7975 are already present in the hosted `scripts/install.sh` on main. If a portable non-`sha256sum` fallback is still wanted, it must pass the wallet as an argument (`python3 -c 'import sys,hashlib; ...' "$wallet"`) or via stdin, never by string interpolation. Happy to review a resubmission built that way.

payload.author: lequangsang01
payload.title: fix(security): harden x86 vintage-arch reward validation against spoofing

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Thank you for taking on #16271 — the word-boundary brand matching and the `cpu_brand_generation_mismatch` regex are exactly the kind of tightening the vintage tiers need, and we'd like to land those. But the central change in `extract_all_features` does the opposite of what the title says, so I have to request changes.

**What the change does**

```python
if check_value.get("passed") is False:
    continue
```

`passed` is a field the *miner* writes into its own fingerprint payload. After this PR, a miner that sets `"passed": false` on a check has that check's raw evidence dropped before the cross-validator ever looks at it. That turns a self-reported flag into an opt-out from validation.

**Measured, same fingerprint, main vs this branch**

Spoof payload: `has_sse2: true, has_avx2: true`, `cv: 0.0004`, flat thermal — modern x86 claiming `i486` — with every check self-marked `passed: false`.

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `simd_consistency` | 0.0 (`disqualifying_feature:has_sse2`, `disqualifying_feature:has_avx2`) | **1.0** (no issue raised) |
| `clock_consistency` | 0.7 (`vintage_arch_i486_too_stable`) | **1.0** (`tsc_less_vintage_expected`) |
| overall | 0.58 | **0.927** |

The new `min(overall_score, 0.2)` cap for disqualifying features only fires when the miner leaves `passed: true` on the SIMD check — so a spoofer just flips the flag and skips the cap entirely.

**The test locks the inversion in** — `node/tests/test_vintage_classifier_anti_spoof.py` lines 44–52:

```python
def test_failed_check_data_ignored():
    """Requirement 2: Checks with passed=False are ignored as evidence."""
    fingerprint = {"checks": {
        "simd_identity": {"passed": False, "data": {"has_sse2": True}},  # Failed check
    }}
    score, details = validate_arch_consistency(fingerprint, "vintage_x86")
    assert "disqualifying_feature:has_sse2" not in details["issues"]
```

This asserts that SSE2 on a machine claiming a 486 is *not* disqualifying as long as the miner says so. Note the honest-486 test (line 10) also relies on `"passed": False` to get its clock data discarded, which is why it passes here and fails on main.

**Direction we'd merge**

1. Never gate evidence on the miner-supplied `passed` flag. Raw `data` is the evidence; the flag is a claim. If anything, `passed: false` with contradictory data should *lower* trust, not remove it.
2. Keep the TSC-less carve-out only if it's paired with positive evidence (e.g. `has_sse2`/`has_avx*` all absent *and* cache tone in the vintage band) — otherwise `cv == 0` becomes a free 1.0.
3. Keep the `\b`-anchored brand matching and the Pentium III/4/Pro/M/D generation regex as-is — those are good.

Also: the branch now conflicts with `main`, so it will need a rebase before it can be re-reviewed. Happy to look again once the evidence path is fixed — the salvageable parts are real improvements.

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Reviewed this against #8087, since you both claim rustchain-bounties#16271. Full adjudication with the test evidence is in one place here so it does not get restated across threads: https://github.com/Scottcjn/rustchain-bounties/issues/16271#issuecomment-5145304675

Headline for this PR: merged into current main it does not change reward behaviour at all. Every spoof case produces byte-identical output to main. arm2 still pays 4.0, nes_6502 still pays 2.8, and the 486 case is clamped by #8022, not by this.

`node/arch_cross_validation.py` is not reachable from the reward path. `derive_verified_device` never calls `validate_arch_consistency`. The only production caller is `run_arch_validation_for_attestation` in `rips/python/rustchain/fleet_immune_system.py`, and nothing calls that except tests. The node's import of that module also fails in a stock checkout:

```
[RIP-201] Fleet immune system not available: No module named 'fleet_immune_system'
```

There is also a regression inside the module you edited. `if check_value.get("passed") is False: continue` lets an attacker hide evidence by marking their own check failed. Modern box claiming i486 with SSE2 and AVX2 present but `simd_identity.passed=false`:

```
main:  score 0.517, issues [disqualifying_feature:has_sse2, has_avx, has_avx2]
8104:  score 0.958, those three issues gone
```

An attacker will always pick passed=false, so on the evasion path that is a net weakening, and `test_failed_check_data_ignored` locks it in.

The brand anchoring and generation-mismatch logic is good reasoning and I would like to see it land, just against `derive_verified_device` in `node/rustchain_v2_integrated_v2.2.1_rip200.py`, which is the function that actually decides the multiplier, and without the passed=False hunk.

Not merging or closing anything, Scott makes the call on payout.

payload.title: fix(nginx): register missing /bcos/, /api/tokenomics, and API routes (closes #7908)

payload.author: qiann0512-gif
payload.body:
This PR is risky to treat as closing #7908 because it does not actually change the `/api/tokenomics` routing path. The current nginx config already has a catch-all `location / { proxy_pass http://rustchain_backend; ... }`, so requests for `/api/tokenomics` were already being proxied to the backend before this patch. The backend route also exists in `node/tokenomics_route.py` and is registered from `node/wsgi.py`.

The diff adds `/api/v1/`, `/api/v2/`, `/bcos`, and several page prefixes, but it never adds or changes an unversioned `/api/tokenomics` location and it does not touch the Flask route registration. So if the live `/api/tokenomics` link is 404ing, this nginx-only change is not evidence that the reported endpoint is fixed; the request would still fall through the same backend path it used before.

Please either add a focused reproduction showing that the old nginx config was the actual blocker for `/api/tokenomics`, or adjust the PR to fix the real deployment/backend registration path for that endpoint. Without that, the PR should not claim to close #7908's `/api/tokenomics` failure.

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Thanks for the macOS work — the underlying problems are real, and your companion PR #8111 fixes them surgically. This one, though, can't go in as-is.

**What the diff actually is**

The `install.sh` in this branch is blob `8e9980ffd37aa7bf06aa1131a6669e10017f3b99`, which is byte-for-byte the current `scripts/install.sh` on `main`. So the PR isn't a rewrite of the root installer; it replaces the root installer with a copy of the older script.

**What that removes from the publicly served installer**

Root `install.sh` (blob `bfa82297e`) is what `curl … | bash` serves. On `main` it has:

- `CHECKSUM_URL` and `file_sha256()` download verification (lines 31, 168) — added in `631a2d0a` "verify installer downloads with checksums"
- `--dry-run` (lines 39, 45, 69) — `abaa301f` "Fix install dry-run side effects"
- `--silent` daemon mode (lines 38, 44)
- the `rustchain.org` default node from `b4a5076c`

None of those survive in this branch (the only `sha256` left is the miner-id derivation on line 605). Shipping unverified downloads from the canonical installer URL is a step backwards we can't take, even for a real portability gain.

**Suggested path**

Close this in favour of #8111 (same author, 7 lines, keeps every safeguard). If `scripts/install.sh` has macOS/bash-3.2 improvements the root one lacks, port those specific hunks onto the root file rather than swapping files. Happy to review that.

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Reviewed against current `main` (merged locally, merge is clean) and ran both full suites.

**This breaks 3 tests in the blocking CI suite, and one of them is a real vintage machine being downgraded.**

The green checks on this PR are misleading: the branch predates `tests/test_device_classification_corpus.py`, which landed with #8023. Merge it into today's main and `tests/` goes from 4 failures to 7:

```
FAILED tests/test_device_classification_corpus.py::test_cited_device_classification_corpus[intel-486-dx2]
FAILED tests/test_device_classification_corpus.py::test_pentium_name_boundaries_do_not_overlap[Intel Pentium 166-modern]
FAILED tests/test_device_classification_corpus.py::test_unrelated_inventory_metadata_does_not_change_classification
```

The 486 one is the serious failure. Corpus entry `intel-486-dx2` is a cited CPUID capture from InstLatx64:

```json
{"family": "x86", "arch": "486", "machine": "i486", "cpu": "Intel 486DX2"}
```

After this PR it classifies as `x86/default` instead of `x86/486`. The brand pattern is `\b(?:i486|80486|486dx|486sx|486)\b`, and none of those alternatives match `486dx2`: `\b486dx\b` fails on the trailing `2`, and `\b486\b` fails because the token continues. So the anti-spoof block rejects a genuine 486 and drops it to the default tier. Real vintage hardware losing its tier is worse than the spoof the PR is closing.

**The new bare-Pentium pattern also catches modern CPUs.** I ran `derive_verified_device` directly on the merged tree:

| CPU brand | main | with this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Intel(R) Pentium(R) Gold G5400 | x86_64/modern (0.8) | x86/pentium (1.5) |
| Intel(R) Pentium(R) Silver N5000 | x86_64/modern (0.8) | x86/pentium (1.5) |
| Intel(R) Pentium(R) CPU G4560 | x86_64/modern (0.8) | x86/pentium (1.5) |
| Intel(R) Pentium(R) 4 CPU 2.40GHz | x86/modern (0.8) | x86/pentium (1.5) |

Two things are going on. The negative lookahead `(?!\s+(?:iii|ii|pro|mmx|m\b|4\b|d\b))` expects whitespace straight after `pentium`, but real Intel brand strings put `(R)` there, so `Pentium(R) 4` slips past the `4` exclusion. And Pentium Gold, Pentium Silver and Pentium Dual-Core are all current or recent parts that the lookahead does not list at all. The `_derive_enroll_weight_device` clamp from #8022 holds the reward at 1.0 rather than 1.5, but that is still up from 0.8 on an honest modern box, and the stored device identity served by the public APIs becomes wrong.

**On the hole this is meant to close.** The x86 half already fails closed on main. I checked with a spoofed payload (`family: x86, arch: 486`, brand `Intel Core i9-13900K`): main derives `x86/486` but `_derive_enroll_weight_device` clamps the reward weight to 1.0, so there is no reward gain today. This PR improves the stored identity for that case, which is worth having, but it is not closing a live reward hole.

**What is still open is the general case, and this PR does not touch it.** `derive_verified_device` ends by returning the claimed family and arch verbatim for any family that is not x86, PowerPC, ARM or exotic, and there is no allowlist of arch values. The new guard is scoped to `family.lower() in ("x86", "x86_64")`, so it does not apply. Measured on both main and this branch, same modern Intel box, fingerprint showing SSE/AVX/AVX2:

| claimed device | resulting weight |
|---|---|
| `{"family": "ARM", "arch": "arm2"}` | 4.0 |
| `{"family": "console", "arch": "nes_6502"}` | 2.8 |
| honest `{"family": "x86_64", "arch": "modern"}` | 0.8 |

`_detect_arm_evidence` returns false because the brand has no ARM token and the reverse check only fires when the claimed family is x86, so the claim falls through untouched and `_derive_enroll_weight_device` only clamps x86 arches. That is a 5x share of a fixed pot on ARM and 3.5x on console, and it survives this PR unchanged.

**Suggested changes**

1. Fix the 486 pattern so `486dx2`, `486dx4`, `486sx2` and similar still match. Something like `\b(?:i?80?486)(?:[a-z]{0,2}\d?)?\b` rather than a fixed

payload.author: waterWang
payload.body:
Per review feedback:
1. Fixed the 486 pattern: changed from `\b(?:i486|80486|486dx|486sx|486)\b` to `\b(?:i?80?486)(?:[a-z]{0,2}\d?)?\b` — now matches `486dx2`, `486dx4`, `486sx2` etc. (the `intel-486-dx2` corpus entry should now classify as `x86/486` instead of `x86/default`)

2. Dropped the bare-Pentium branch entirely — as you noted, `Intel Pentium 166` is correctly classified as `modern` on main, and the bare pattern catches modern CPUs like Pentium Gold/Silver that carry `(R)` in the brand string. A separate PR can update the corpus if vintage P5 classification is desired.

3. The `(R)` issue in the lookahead is moot since the bare-Pentium branch is removed.

The remaining ARM/console spoofing (suggested fix #4) would be a separate follow-up PR.

Please run `python -m pytest tests/ -q` against the rebased branch to verify the 3 previously-failing tests now pass.

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
Reviewed this against #8104, since you both claim rustchain-bounties#16271. Full adjudication with the test evidence is in one place here so it does not get restated across threads: https://github.com/Scottcjn/rustchain-bounties/issues/16271#issuecomment-5145304675

Headline for this PR: it is the closer of the two and it is on the right function, but it is not mergeable as written. Merged into current main it downgrades genuine vintage silicon:

```
Intel 486DX2-66     2.0 -> 1.0
Am486DX4-100        2.0 -> 1.0
Intel i486SX 25MHz  2.0 -> 1.0
Intel 80386DX 33MHz 2.5 -> 1.0
```

Two regex bugs. In `\b(?:i?80?486)(?:[a-z]{0,2}\d?)?\b` the 8 in `80?` is not optional, so the pattern only ever matches `80486`. And in the brand check `\b(?:i486|80486|486dx|486sx|486)\b` every alternative needs word boundaries on both ends, which `486dx2`, `i486sx` and `am486dx4` all fail.

That shows up in the blocking suite: `tests/` goes from 4 pre-existing failures on main to 6, and one of the new ones is `test_cited_device_classification_corpus[intel-486-dx2]`, the captured real 486DX2.

Fix the patterns so 486DX2, i486SX, Am486DX4 and 80386DX all keep their tiers, get that corpus test green, and this becomes mergeable. The SIMD corroboration half is sound as written. Also please correct the body: it says Am486DX4 is handled and that there is no blast radius outside the enroll-weight path, and neither is true.

Not merging or closing anything, Scott makes the call on payout.

payload.body:
Reviewed. **The bug is real and the fix is the right shape** — but this is escrow logic on a production chain, so it is not merging on my authority. Detail below so the human review is short.

### The trap you found is genuine

I traced the state machine on current `main`. `/dispute` sets `status = 'disputed'` and answers the client with "Worker can re-deliver." Then:

- `/deliver` gated on `if j["status"] != STATUS_CLAIMED: → 409`
- **no route anywhere moves a job from `disputed` back to `claimed`**

So the message is telling the worker to do something the API refuses. Meanwhile the escrow stays locked, and — as you note — a disputed job sits outside the expiry sweep, so it does not even time out into a refund. The only reachable exit is the poster cancelling and recovering the full escrow, *after* the deliverable is already readable on the public job endpoint. That is a real economic asymmetry, not just a UX dead end: it lets a poster dispute-then-cancel and keep both the work and the money.

### The fix reads correctly

Three things I specifically checked rather than skimmed:

1. **The CAS still holds.** You did not weaken the optimistic-concurrency guard — `expected_status = STATUS_DISPUTED if redelivery else STATUS_CLAIMED` keeps `WHERE job_id = ? AND status = ?` a real compare-and-swap, with the `rowcount == 0 → STATE_RACE` rollback intact. This is the thing I most expected to find broken, and it isn't.
2. **The TTL carve-out is justified, not convenient.** Skipping the expiry gate on re-delivery is correct *because* `_expire_refundable_job` ignores disputed jobs — otherwise a re-delivery after the original TTL would fail with a misleading `STATE_RACE`. Your comment says exactly that, and the code does exactly what the comment says.
3. **`rejection_reason = ''` on re-delivery** is right — a stale rejection reason next to a fresh deliverable would be actively misleading. Logging `redelivered` distinctly from `delivered` keeps the audit trail honest about which path ran.

The `/dispute` message now naming the concrete routes (`POST /agent/jobs/<id>/deliver`, `POST /agent/jobs/<id>/cancel`) instead of vague prose is a small thing that will save real support time.

### BLOCKED-for-human — needs @Scottcjn

RIP-302 job escrow is money movement. Standing rule here is that reward, consensus, wallet, attestation, and settlement paths do not merge on a reviewer's word alone, however clean the diff. The review above is a **recommendation to merge**.

Two questions for the human, both genuine policy rather than code:

- **Unbounded dispute→re-deliver cycles.** Nothing limits how many times a poster can dispute and a worker re-deliver. That is arguably correct (it mirrors real revision rounds), but it means a job can stay escrowed indefinitely with no terminal state. Worth deciding whether a re-delivery cap or a dispute-window deadline belongs here.
- **Does re-delivery restart any review clock?** `delivered_at` is overwritten, which is probably what you want, but if anything downstream measures poster response time from `delivered_at`, a re-delivery silently resets it.

### One housekeeping note

**PR #8186 contains this entire diff.** Its file list is `rip302_agent_economy.py` (23+/7-) and `tests/test_agent_dispute_redelivery.py` (254+/0-) — byte-identical to this PR — *plus* two wallet files. So #8186 is a superset of this PR under a title that only mentions the wallet change. Whichever lands first, the other needs rebasing, and #8186 should not be merged as a "wallet fix" while quietly carrying escrow changes. Flagged on #8186 as well. Not your fault that the branches stacked this way after the backlog pass, but the human merging needs to know before clicking.

Thank you for this one — a dispute path that strands escrow is exactly the class of bug worth finding.

Checked this against the current `.github/workflows/stale.yml` and against the `actions/stale` v10 semantics. It does the right thing.

The key line is `days-before-close: -1`, which disables closing. Because `days-before-pr-close: 14` is set explicitly, the PR side still closes and only the issue side falls back to the `-1`. So the resulting behaviour is:

- Issues: labelled `stale` after 45 days of inactivity, commented on, never auto-closed.
- PRs: labelled `stale` after 21 days, closed 14 days later.

That is the shape I would want. Dropping `close-issue-message` is consistent, since issues no longer close.

Two things I checked that are worth noting:

`security` was already in `exempt-issue-labels` on main, so an exempt label was not what failed. Whatever got auto-closed was not carrying the label at the time. That is an argument for the `-1` doing the real work here rather than the label list, which is how this PR is built. Adding `consensus,tracking,operations` is still useful as a second layer.

`operations-per-run` going 50 to 300 is the one change with a cost. It is six times the GitHub API budget per run, on a repo with a lot of open issues and PRs. It should be fine at a weekly cadence, but if the job starts hitting rate limits that is the first knob to turn back down.

No test impact, this is workflow-only. Looks good to me.

payload.author: qiann0512-gif
payload.body:
The evidence/no-evidence split is the right direction, but this still leaves the bypass alive when all active checks are unmeasured. After the patch, `measured_count == 0` still sets `active_ratio = 1.0`, and both enrollment paths multiply reward weight by that ratio (`hw_weight * rotation_eval["active_ratio"]` / `rotation_eval['active_ratio']`).

So a payload where every active check is `{"passed": true}` without usable `data` now produces `active_results` of all `None`, `active_total` of 0, and `active_ratio` of 1.0. That is exactly the no-evidence case described in the PR: it no longer increments `active_pass_count`, but the downstream weight calculation can still treat it as full credit because it only uses the ratio.

Please make the zero-measured-check case fail closed for reward weighting, or carry an explicit "no measured evidence" flag that enrollment treats as no rotating-check reward. A regression should cover a fingerprint with only dict `passed: true` / no `data` entries and assert that the resulting enrollment weight does not get full `hw_weight` credit.

payload.author: Scottcjn
payload.body:
The direction here is right and it matches the standing rule for this code, that the server does not trust `"passed": true` without raw evidence. Splitting unmeasured from failed is the correct model: hardware that genuinely cannot measure a check should not be punished the same as a client that skipped it.

One thing to resolve before this goes in, because I think it leaves the strongest version of the attack open.

```python
active_ratio = (len(passed_active) / measured_count) if measured_count else 1.0
```

Consider a client that submits **every** active check as `{"passed": true}` with no `data`. Each one maps to `None`, `measured` ends up empty, `measured_count` is `0`, and the ratio falls through to the `else` branch and becomes **1.0, a perfect score**.

That is the same 1.0 such a client gets on `main` today, so this is not a regression. But it means the bypass this PR is aimed at still succeeds in its most complete form. The PR closes the mixed case, where some checks carry evidence and others do not, and leaves the all-evidence-omitted case scoring perfectly. An attacker picks the version that works.

An empty denominator is not "everything passed", it is "nothing was proven", and those should not score the same. Options, your call which fits the protocol:

- treat `measured_count == 0` as `0.0` rather than `1.0`
- or reject the attestation outright, in the same shape as an unmeasurable-hardware case, so it is visible rather than silently perfect
- and either way, a test pinning the all-unmeasured case, since that is the one the current tests do not cover

Please also add tests for the three-way split: measured-pass, measured-fail, and unmeasured. Changing `_fingerprint_check_passed` from `bool` to a tri-state return is the kind of signature change where a later reader can easily reintroduce a truthiness bug, given `None` and `False` are both falsy.

Worth saying: catching that unmeasured and failed were being conflated is a good find, and the docstring you added is clear. It is the empty-denominator default that needs to change.
